To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
(i) the number of middle authors in biomedical research is increasing, and (ii) middle authors are contributing increasingly more to the overall production in the biomedical field.

(1) the number of middle authors in the by-line is positively correlated to the total number of authors in an article, (2) middle authors are not secondary contributors but are, rather, equally involved in the production of knowledge as the primary authors and the supervisory authors, and (3) the relative importance of middle authors in biomedical research has increased over time.
the division of labor and the relative credit of authors in biomedical research has changed significantly over the last 30 years, and that middle authors have become increasingly more important.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the proper allocation of credit and responsibility in biomedical research.
the division of labor in biomedical research and how it affects the attribution of credit to the authors of scientific publications.
the proper allocation of credit in collaborative biomedical research.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the rise in the number of authors per article is due to an increased division of labor and collaboration in biomedical research, which is a consequence of the increasing complexity and size of biomedical research projects.
the middle authors are becoming more important, but not necessarily more important than the first and last ones.
the rise of the middle author is not due to an increasing number of secondary contributors, but to a growing importance of the middle authors in the production of biomedical knowledge.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the middle authors of biomedical research have been gaining in relative importance over time.

the division of labor and the credit attribution in biomedical research are becoming more complex, with a significant proportion of the research team members contributing to the production of knowledge in a way that does not allow for a straightforward distinction between primary and secondary contributions.
the middle authors are not middle authors anymore, they are now the primary authors.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, in the current authorship practices, the distinction between first and middle authors is not meaningful, and the division of labor in research teams cannot be properly inferred from the byline.

, although middle authors do not contribute less than the first or last authors to biomedical research, the current practice of attributing them less credit and responsibility for the results of research is not justified by the data.

the current practice of listing authors alphabetically does not reflect the actual division and allocation of credit and responsibilities in research teams, and should therefore be abandoned in order to improve the fairness and transparency of authorship practices in the biomedical sciences.
